Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it

vignette: Sara, a 32-year-old South Asian woman and nurse, has been struggling with the aftermath of a devastating man-made disaster that occurred at her hospital nearly six months ago. The event was an explosion caused by a gas leak in one of the supply rooms, leading to a fire that spread quickly through multiple floors of the building. Sara was working in the ER when it happened and had to navigate through smoke-filled corridors to help evacuate patients and colleagues. The memory of that day feels surreal to her-so extreme that she often has trouble believing it actually happened to her. The moments are fragmented, with disconnected pieces that do not fit together seamlessly. One memory is of hearing a sudden loud bang followed by the smell of burning plastic; another is of feeling the heat on her skin as she tried to make her way through the chaos. However, these pieces often feel disjointed and don't create a coherent narrative in her mind. Sara has also found herself pushing away parts of the memory before she can fully recall them, which leaves gaps in her understanding of what exactly transpired that day. This blocking makes it difficult for her to piece together the sequence of events or understand how certain things happened. For example, she remembers helping a patient down several flights of stairs but cannot remember if there were others who assisted with this task. In her daily work as a nurse, Sara is often reminded of these fragmented memories. The smell of antiseptic in the hospital can suddenly trigger a flash of that overwhelming smoke, or hearing an ambulance siren can transport her back to the chaos of that day. These triggers disrupt her focus and leave her feeling disoriented and disconnected from her surroundings. Sara's work as a nurse has become increasingly challenging because of these memories. She finds it difficult to concentrate during shifts, often pausing in the middle of tasks when fragments of the disaster come flooding back. This lack of continuity in her memory has made her feel less confident in her abilities, and she worries about making mistakes due to her distraction. Her colleagues have noticed a change in Sara's demeanor; she seems more distant and distracted during rounds. While they offer support, Sara often pushes them away because she doesn't want to burden others with her struggles. This isolation has left her feeling increasingly alone in her experience. Despite these challenges, what frightens Sara most is the sense of disconnection from reality that comes with these fragmented memories. She worries about losing touch with who she was before the disaster and whether she can ever fully reclaim a coherent understanding of herself and her experiences. The prospect of continuing to live with these disjointed pieces haunts her. It was this persistent feeling of unreality, coupled with the growing impact on her work and relationships, that finally compelled Sara to seek help. She is most hopeful for a way to make sense of what happened-to integrate those fragmented memories into a more coherent narrative. Ultimately, she wants to regain a sense of normalcy and confidence in her ability to function both at work and in her personal life. Sara's journey to therapy represents a step toward reclaiming control over her thoughts and experiences, hoping to find a way through the disorienting fragments that have been disrupting her daily life.
